vignette:
He was seven years old when they left. The details have blurred around the edges, but certain images remain sharp and indelible—the rough texture of his father’s hand pulling him through a checkpoint at dusk, the smell of diesel and wet wool, the sight of his mother pressing a silver Kiddush cup into the lining of a suitcase. They were part of a convoy of Jewish families fleeing a city that had become a trap. He remembers the sound of distant explosions, and the way the grown-ups whispered in a language he wasn’t supposed to understand. Arriving in a new country—North America—was supposed to be the end of fear. He learned English, changed his name slightly, became a rabbi. That was the story he told himself.

But the fear never really left. Now, at sixty-three, he lives in a quiet suburban community with his wife of thirty-five years, leads a congregation of about two hundred families, and spends most of his waking hours helping others navigate their grief, their doubts, their fractures. He is good at it. They call him compassionate, wise. And he is. But there is a part of him that nobody sees—not even his wife.

It shows up in small ways. He cannot stand the sound of sirens. When an ambulance passes during a Shabbat service, he loses his train of thought for a full minute, his hands trembling as he grips the bimah. He has learned to pause, take a sip of water, pretend it is a moment of reflection. Inside, his heart pounds like it did when he was a child and a soldier’s flashlight swept across the car they were hiding in. He avoids news reports about refugee camps, about displaced families. He tells himself it is too painful to witness, but the truth is he is afraid of what he will feel—the old panic, the shame of having survived.

His sleep has been poor for years. He wakes at three in the morning, drenched, the image of his grandmother’s face—left behind, never seen again—floating in the dark above the bed. He does not tell his wife about these nightmares. She knows something is wrong, but when she asks, he says, “Just a long day.” She has learned not to push.

At work, he has begun to dread certain questions. When a congregant asks him to speak about his own journey of faith during the Holocaust memorial service, he deflects. “Let’s focus on the survivors we honor,” he says, though he knows the real reason: he cannot stand in front of a microphone and talk about what it means to be a refugee without the tears coming, without his voice breaking. He feels a constant, low-grade vigilance. In crowded rooms—during a bar mitzvah reception, a board meeting—he scans for exits. He stands with his back to the wall. He tells himself it is habit. But his body remembers what his mind tries to forget.

Recently, during a counseling session with a young couple who had fled a war zone, he found himself unable to speak. Their story was too close. He excused himself, went to his office, and sat shaking for ten minutes. He thought about his own mother, who never spoke about the journey, who died of a heart attack at fifty-two. He wonders sometimes if she died of grief.

His relationship is the one place he feels safest, and yet the most exposed. His wife holds him at night, but he cannot tell her why he flinches when she touches his shoulder from behind. He cannot tell her that part of him is still running. Instead, he pours himself into his work, into the familiar rhythms of prayer and community, hoping the structure will hold him together. It does—barely. But the past is a living thing inside him, and it does not observe the boundaries of time or geography. It arrives without warning, in the middle of a sermon, in the smell of wet wool on a rainy morning, in the silence between two words of a blessing.
